title: Digital Systems & Computer Hardware
blurb: How physical electronic components become digital computing systems -- practical and visual, not a Linear Circuits course.

intermediate: Storing one bit and many bits

description: How physical electronic components -- transistors, gates, registers, memory -- combine into digital computing systems. Practical, visual, simulation-based; not a Linear Circuits or electrical-engineering theory course.

lessons.title: From electricity to digital information
objectives: Explain why binary states are represented by voltage ranges, not exact values
Explain how voltage changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect voltage with ground and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Voltage is an electrical level measured relative to a reference point called ground. Current is the flow of charge, and resistance limits how much current flows for a given voltage -- components heat up because resistance converts some electrical energy into heat.
examples:
# conceptual, not a real measurement:
# 'digital 1' on a 5V system might mean: anything from 2.0V to 5.0V
# 'digital 0' might mean: anything from 0V to 0.8V
# voltages between 0.8V and 2.0V are ambiguous -- a well-designed circuit
# never lets a signal sit there for long
commonMistakes: Assuming a digital '1' means exactly one specific voltage -- it's actually a RANGE, which is exactly why real digital systems tolerate some electrical noise without misreading a signal.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the foundational mental model for everything else in digital hardware -- registers, memory, and processors are all built from this one idea, repeated billions of times.

lessons.title: Transistors as switches
objectives: Explain how a transistor acts as an electronically controlled switch
Explain how transistor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect transistor with MOSFET and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A transistor is a component that can be turned on or off by an electrical signal, functioning as a switch with no moving parts. A simplified MOSFET has three connections: when a control signal is applied to one, current can flow between the other two (on); without it, current can't flow (off).
examples:
# conceptual switch behavior, not real semiconductor physics:
# control_signal = HIGH  -> switch is ON  -> current flows
# control_signal = LOW   -> switch is OFF -> current blocked
# combining many switches in specific patterns creates every digital component covered later in this course
commonMistakes: Expecting to need semiconductor physics or equations to understand this -- the switch BEHAVIOR is all you need; the physics of exactly why it switches is a separate, much deeper topic this.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding 'it's just switches, arranged cleverly' demystifies processors -- the complexity is in the ARRANGEMENT, not exotic components.
lessons.explain: A transistor is a component that can be turned on or off by an electrical signal, functioning as a switch with no moving parts. A simplified MOSFET has three connections: when a control signal is applied to one, current can flow between the other two (on); without it, current can't flow (off).

# conceptual switch behavior, not real semiconductor physics:
# control_signal = HIGH  -> switch is ON  -> current flows
# control_signal = LOW   -> switch is OFF -> current blocked
# combining many switches in specific patterns creates every digital component covered later in this course

lessons.title: Real digital signals
objectives: Explain floating inputs, pull-up/down resistors, and why timing matters in real circuits
Explain how floating input changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect floating input with pull-up resistor and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A floating input is one connected to nothing definite -- it can read as random noise instead of a clean 0 or 1, causing unpredictable behavior. A pull-up or pull-down resistor solves this by gently forcing an unconnected input toward a known state (high or low) when nothing else is driving it.
examples:
# floating input problem: an unconnected switch input might read as
# 0 or 1 unpredictably, flickering between them from electrical noise
# fix: a pull-down resistor gently pulls it LOW when nothing else drives it,
# so it reads a clean, predictable 0 until something actively drives it HIGH
commonMistakes: Assuming an unconnected digital input reads as a safe default -- without a pull-up or pull-down resistor, it can read as EITHER value unpredictably, which is a genuinely common source of.
lessons.careerRelevance: Floating-input bugs and active-low mix-ups are two of the most common real hardware debugging scenarios -- covered again explicitly in the Hardware Debugging lesson.

lessons.title: Fundamental digital components
objectives: Describe what each basic gate does, as a physical hardware block
Explain how NOT gate changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect NOT gate with AND gate and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Gates are the smallest reusable hardware building blocks: NOT flips a single signal (on becomes off, off becomes on). AND only outputs on when BOTH inputs are on.
examples:
# thinking in terms of behavior, not formal notation:
# AND gate: output is ON only when input_1 AND input_2 are both ON
# OR gate:  output is ON when input_1 OR input_2 (or both) are ON
# XOR gate: output is ON only when the two inputs are DIFFERENT from each other
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize gates as abstract symbolic rules -- it's far more useful (and how this course treats them) to think of each as a physical component you can toggle and observe directly in.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every combinational circuit in later lessons (adders, multiplexers, decoders) is built entirely from these six gate types, combined in different arrangements.

# OR gate:  output is ON when input_1 OR input_2 (or both) are ON
# XOR gate: output is ON only when the two inputs are DIFFERENT from each other

lessons.title: Combinational systems
objectives: Explain what multiplexers, demultiplexers, encoders, and decoders each route or select
Explain how multiplexer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect multiplexer with demultiplexer and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A multiplexer (mux) selects ONE of several data inputs to pass through, based on a separate select signal -- like a rotary switch choosing which of several inputs reaches the output. A demultiplexer does the reverse: routes one input to one of several outputs, based on a select signal.
examples:
# 4-to-1 multiplexer, conceptually:
# inputs = [A, B, C, D], select = 2  ->  output = C
# (the select signal literally picks which input line reaches the output)
commonMistakes: Confusing an encoder with a decoder -- an encoder COMPRESSES many possible inputs into a compact code; a decoder EXPANDS a compact code back into many individual output lines.
lessons.careerRelevance: Multiplexers specifically show up constantly in real datapaths -- the CPU-building lessons later in this course rely on them directly to select which value flows where.

lessons.title: Binary arithmetic hardware
objectives: Trace how a half adder and full adder combine to add multi-bit binary numbers
Explain how half adder changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect half adder with full adder and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A half adder takes two single bits and produces a sum bit and a carry bit (for when both inputs are 1, needing to 'carry' into the next position -- exactly like carrying a 1 in decimal addition).
examples:
# adding two 4-bit numbers, bit by bit, like manual long addition:
# each bit-position's full adder takes: bit_a, bit_b, carry_in
# and produces: sum_bit, carry_out (which becomes the NEXT position's carry_in)
# 4-bit example: 0111 (7) + 1001 (9) = overflow, since 16 needs 5 bits
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a carry from one bit position must feed into the NEXT position's addition -- this chaining is exactly what makes multi-bit addition work, and is exactly what the 4-bit adder.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every arithmetic operation a CPU performs ultimately reduces to circuits built from full adders chained together this way.

lessons.title: Clocks and timing
objectives: Explain what a clock signal is and why faster clocks aren't automatically better
Explain how clock signal changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect clock signal with clock cycle and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A clock is a signal that alternates between high and low at a steady rate, providing a shared heartbeat that synchronizes when circuits update. A rising edge (low-to-high transition) or falling edge is often the exact moment storage elements update their values.
examples:
# why clock speed has limits, conceptually:
# if the slowest signal path takes 3 nanoseconds to settle,
# the clock period must be AT LEAST slightly more than 3ns --
# otherwise the next clock edge arrives before the signal has finished settling,
# and the wrong (not-yet-settled) value gets captured
commonMistakes: Assuming a faster clock is always strictly better -- if the critical path can't keep up, a faster clock causes real, hard-to-diagnose timing failures rather than faster correct operation.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding critical-path limits is exactly why real processors can't simply be clocked arbitrarily fast -- a genuine, practical engineering constraint.

lessons.title: Storing one bit and many bits
objectives: Explain why combinational circuits alone cannot remember, and how flip-flops and registers do
Explain how latch changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect latch with flip-flop and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A purely combinational circuit's output depends ONLY on its current inputs -- it has no memory of the past. A latch or flip-flop is different: it can hold ('store') a value, changing only at specific moments (like a clock edge), and holding steady otherwise.
examples:
# a 1-bit storage element's behavior, conceptually:
# on a clock edge: if reset is active, value becomes 0
#                  else if enable is active, value becomes the current input
#                  else, value stays exactly as it was (this is the 'memory' part)
commonMistakes: Assuming any circuit can just 'remember' a value automatically -- memory requires a DELIBERATE storage element (a flip-flop or register); wires and gates alone have no memory at all.
lessons.careerRelevance: This enable/reset/clock pattern is exactly what the Register and Clock Simulator lets you interact with directly later in this course.

lessons.title: Counters and state machines
objectives: Explain how a counter and a finite-state machine both use registers to track change over time
Explain how counter changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect counter with finite-state machine and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A counter is a register that increases (or decreases) its stored value by a fixed amount on each clock pulse, cycling through a sequence of values.
examples:
# a simple 3-state traffic light FSM, described as a diagram, not formulas:
# STATE red    --(timer expires)--> STATE green
# STATE green  --(timer expires)--> STATE yellow
# STATE yellow --(timer expires)--> STATE red
# exactly one state is active at any moment; the diagram shows every possible transition
commonMistakes: Trying to reduce a state machine down to formal Boolean equations -- this course deliberately treats FSMs as DIAGRAMS (states and transitions you can trace visually), which is how most real.
lessons.careerRelevance: State machines appear constantly in real hardware and software alike -- from traffic-light controllers to network protocol handling to game logic.

lessons.title: Memory systems
objectives: Distinguish registers, cache, RAM, and storage, and explain how a CPU addresses memory
Explain how memory hierarchy changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect memory hierarchy with address lines and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Memory exists in a hierarchy by speed, size, and cost: registers (fastest, tiniest, right on the CPU), cache (small and fast), RAM (larger, slower, holds a running program's data), and storage/disk (largest, slowest, persists after power off).
examples:
# reading from memory, conceptually:
# 1. CPU puts the desired address on the address lines
# 2. CPU sets the 'read' control signal active
# 3. memory responds by placing the stored data at that address
#    onto the data lines, for the CPU to read
commonMistakes: Confusing 'more memory' with 'faster memory' -- the hierarchy exists specifically because faster memory is far more expensive per bit, so systems use a small amount of very fast memory.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the SAME memory hierarchy concept covered from the software/OS side in the Computer Architecture course -- this lesson explains how the hardware itself is actually built and addressed.

lessons.title: Datapaths and ALUs
objectives: Trace how registers, a bus, a multiplexer, and an ALU combine into a working datapath
Explain how datapath changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect datapath with bus and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A datapath is the arrangement of registers, buses (shared wires carrying data between components), multiplexers (selecting which value flows where), and an ALU (performing the actual computation) that together move and transform data under the direction of control signals.
examples:
# tracing one operation through a datapath, conceptually:
# 1. control signals select Register A and Register B as ALU inputs (via multiplexers)
# 2. control signal selects 'ADD' as the ALU operation
# 3. ALU computes A + B
# 4. control signal selects Register C as the destination
# 5. on the next clock edge, Register C stores the ALU's result
commonMistakes: Assuming each operation needs its OWN dedicated circuit -- the whole point of a datapath is REUSING the same registers, bus, and ALU for many different operations, just with different.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is the direct bridge between individual hardware components and the 'tiny processor' built in the next lesson -- and connects directly to how the Computer Architecture course describes CPU behavior at a higher level.

lessons.title: Building a tiny processor
objectives: Trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle through a small, concrete instruction set
Explain how program counter changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect program counter with instruction register and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A tiny processor combines everything from this course: a program counter (tracks which instruction is next), an instruction register (holds the current instruction being processed), a small set of general registers, and an ALU -- all connected by a datapath.
examples:
# fetch-decode-execute, one instruction at a time:
# FETCH:   read instruction at program_counter, e.g. "ADD R2, R0, R1"
# DECODE:  operation=ADD, destination=R2, sources=R0 and R1
# EXECUTE: R2 = R0 + R1 (using the ALU and datapath from the previous lessons)
# advance program_counter, repeat
commonMistakes: Confusing this course's focus (how the hardware BLOCKS are built and connected) with the Computer Architecture course's focus (how a COMPLETED processor and operating system behave).
lessons.careerRelevance: This is quite literally 'how a CPU works' at the most concrete, traceable level -- exactly the kind of systems-fundamentals question that comes up in technical interviews.
lessons.explain: A tiny processor combines everything from this course: a program counter (tracks which instruction is next), an instruction register (holds the current instruction being processed), a small set of general registers, and an ALU -- all connected by a datapath.

lessons.title: Hardware interfaces
objectives: Distinguish GPIO, UART, SPI, and I²C at the signal level, and when each is used
Explain how GPIO changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect GPIO with UART and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: GPIO (General Purpose Input/Output) pins can be individually configured as simple digital inputs or outputs -- the most basic way a processor reads a switch or drives an LED. UART is a simple serial protocol sending one bit at a time over a single wire pair, commonly used for basic device-to-device communication.
examples:
# choosing an interface, conceptually:
# one on/off LED or button -> GPIO is simplest, no protocol needed
# two devices, simple messages, few wires -> UART
# one fast device, dedicated wires available -> SPI
# several devices sharing very few wires, each with an address -> I2C
commonMistakes: Assuming one interface is universally 'best' -- each is a genuine trade-off between speed, wire count, and how many devices need to share the connection; the right choice depends on the.
lessons.careerRelevance: This lesson deliberately keeps hardware-interface depth shallow -- detailed microcontroller programming with these interfaces belongs in the planned Embedded Systems & Microcontrollers course.

lessons.title: Hardware debugging
objectives: Recognize common real hardware faults from their symptoms
Explain how floating input changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect floating input with reset polarity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real hardware faults tend to fall into recognizable patterns: a floating input reads unpredictably because nothing is driving it firmly. Incorrect reset polarity means a circuit designed for active-low reset gets an active-high signal (or vice versa), so it never resets when expected -- or resets constantly.
examples:
# recognizing symptoms, conceptually:
# 'this register never seems to update' -> check: is enable actually reaching it? is the clock reaching it?
# 'this circuit resets at the wrong times' -> check: active-high vs active-low reset polarity mismatch
# 'random/flickering behavior on this input' -> check: is it floating (missing a pull-up/pull-down)?
commonMistakes: Assuming a hardware bug must be exotic -- the vast majority of real digital hardware faults are exactly these few recognizable patterns, which is why this lesson lists them explicitly rather.
lessons.careerRelevance: This pattern-recognition approach mirrors the Debugging course's own philosophy, applied specifically to hardware rather than software.

quiz.q: Why isn't a digital '1' one exact voltage value?
options: It is exactly one value on every system
Real signals are represented as voltage RANGES, with a forbidden zone in between
Digital signals don't use voltage at all
'1' only exists in software, not hardware

quiz.q: What does a transistor do, functionally, in digital hardware?
options: Acts as an electronically controlled switch (on/off)

quiz.q: What problem does a floating input cause?
options: It can read as an unpredictable value since nothing firmly drives it
It always reads as a clean 0

quiz.q: What does a pull-down resistor do?
options: Gently forces an unconnected input toward a known LOW state

quiz.q: What does 'active-low' mean for a signal?
options: The signal triggers its action when it reads LOW (0), not high
The signal only works at low clock speeds

quiz.q: What does propagation delay refer to?
options: How long a program takes to compile
How long a signal takes to travel and settle after an input changes
Selects one of several data inputs to pass through, based on a select signal
Converts serial to parallel data only

quiz.q: In a full adder, what does the carry-in represent?
options: The carry produced by the PREVIOUS bit position's addition

quiz.q: Why can't a purely combinational circuit remember a value?
options: Its output depends only on CURRENT inputs, with no storage element to hold a past value
It's too slow to remember anything

quiz.q: What does a register's 'enable' signal control?
options: Whether the whole chip is powered on
Whether the register actually updates its stored value on the next clock edge

quiz.q: On a clock edge, what happens if reset is active?
options: The stored value is forced back to a known reset state, typically 0

quiz.q: What is a finite-state machine, conceptually?
options: A system that's always in exactly one state, moving to a new state based on current state and inputs

quiz.q: Why does memory exist in a hierarchy (registers, cache, RAM, storage)?
options: It's a historical accident with no real reason
Faster memory is far more expensive per bit, so systems combine a little very-fast memory with much more slower memory
All memory types are equally fast

quiz.q: In the fetch-decode-execute cycle, what does 'fetch' do?
options: Retrieves the next instruction, using the program counter to know where

quiz.q: Which hardware interface uses just two shared wires for many devices, each with its own address?
What commonly causes a register to appear 'frozen,' never updating?
options: A missing or incorrect enable signal reaching it

quiz.q: What does the 'critical path' refer to in timing analysis?
options: The shortest signal path in a circuit
The SLOWEST signal path, which limits how fast the clock can safely run
A path that only exists during reset
The path data takes through memory only

quiz.q: What does this course's simulations honestly represent?
options: Real analog circuit behavior with full precision
Deterministic, simplified digital models -- not literal analog circuit simulation

exercises.title: Identify a floating input
exercises.prompt: A digital input pin is connected to nothing else and randomly flickers between reading 0 and 1. What is this problem called, and what's the standard fix?
exercises.hint: a floating input; fixed with a pull-up or pull-down resistor to give it a defined default state

exercises.title: Choose pull-up or pull-down
exercises.prompt: You want an unconnected button input to default to reading 0 (LOW) until the button is pressed. Would you use a pull-up or pull-down resistor?
exercises.hint: a pull-down resistor, since it forces the default state toward LOW (0)

exercises.title: Predict an active-low reset
exercises.prompt: A component's reset input is active-low, but the circuit driving it holds the line HIGH by default and only pulls it LOW briefly during a fault. Under normal operation, is the component held in reset or allowed to run?
exercises.hint: allowed to run -- active-low reset only triggers when the line goes LOW, and it's HIGH under normal operation

exercises.title: Select the correct digital component
exercises.prompt: You need one input out of eight to be selected and routed to a single output, based on a 3-bit select code. Which component do you need?
exercises.hint: a multiplexer (specifically an 8-to-1 mux, since 3 select bits can address 8 inputs)

exercises.title: Route a multiplexer
exercises.prompt: Given a 4-to-1 multiplexer with inputs [A=10, B=20, C=30, D=40] and select=1, what value reaches the output?
exercises.hint: 20 (select=1 picks the second input, B, using 0-indexing)

exercises.title: Trace a multi-bit adder
exercises.prompt: Add the 4-bit binary values 0110 (6) and 0011 (3) using a chain of full adders. What is the 4-bit result and is there a carry-out?
exercises.hint: 1001 (9), no carry-out, since 6+3=9 fits within 4 bits (max 15)

exercises.title: Detect overflow
exercises.prompt: Adding two 4-bit values 1111 (15) and 0001 (1) produces what result, and does it overflow a 4-bit register?
exercises.hint: the true sum is 16, which needs 5 bits -- so yes, it overflows a 4-bit register (the stored result would incorrectly show 0000 with a carry-out of 1)

exercises.title: Trace register contents across clock edges
exercises.prompt: A register starts at 0. On clock edge 1: enable=1, input=5. On clock edge 2: enable=0, input=9. On clock edge 3: enable=1, input=7. What is the register's value after each edge?
exercises.hint: after edge 1: 5 (enabled, takes input). after edge 2: 5 (not enabled, unchanged). after edge 3: 7 (enabled, takes new input)

exercises.title: Diagnose why a counter does not advance
exercises.prompt: A binary counter is supposed to increment every clock cycle but stays frozen at its current value. List two plausible hardware causes.
exercises.hint: the clock signal isn't actually reaching the counter, or the enable signal is stuck low/inactive

exercises.title: Read a timing diagram
exercises.prompt: A timing diagram shows a clock signal rising at time T, and a data signal changing shortly AFTER T on every cycle. Is the data signal likely being captured correctly on that clock edge?
exercises.hint: likely NOT reliably -- data should be stable and settled BEFORE the clock edge (respecting setup time), not changing shortly after it

exercises.title: Repair an incorrect enable connection
exercises.prompt: A register's enable input is accidentally wired directly to ground (permanently 0/inactive) instead of to the intended control signal. What visible symptom would this cause?
exercises.hint: the register would never update, appearing permanently frozen at whatever value it happened to hold on startup

exercises.title: Diagnose reset polarity
exercises.prompt: A flip-flop expects an active-high reset, but the circuit was built assuming active-low reset logic. What would you observe?
exercises.hint: the flip-flop would reset constantly (since the line is normally LOW, which the flip-flop wrongly reads as its OWN active-high trigger) or never reset at all, depending on which way the mismatch runs

exercises.title: Trace data through a datapath
exercises.prompt: A datapath's control signals select Register A and Register B as ALU inputs, ADD as the operation, and Register C as the destination. If A=4 and B=6, what value does Register C hold after the next clock edge?
exercises.hint: 10 (4+6), stored into Register C on the clock edge

exercises.title: Identify the next processor state
exercises.prompt: A tiny processor's program counter is at instruction 2 of a 4-instruction program (LOAD, LOAD, ADD, HALT). After executing the ADD instruction, what happens to the program counter and what executes next?
exercises.hint: the program counter advances to instruction 3, and the HALT instruction executes next, stopping the processor

exercises.title: Choose between UART, SPI, and I²C
exercises.prompt: You need to connect six sensors to a microcontroller using as few wires as possible, and speed isn't critical. Which interface fits best, and why?
exercises.hint: I²C -- it supports many addressed devices on just two shared wires, trading speed for minimal wiring, which matches this scenario's priorities

exercises.title: Diagnose a chip-select problem
exercises.prompt: Two SPI devices share the same data lines but their chip-select signals are accidentally both wired active at the same time. What symptom would this likely cause?
exercises.hint: both devices try to respond simultaneously on the shared data line, causing conflicting/garbled data (bus contention) rather than a clean response from either device

exercises.title: Find a signal-arrival timing problem
exercises.prompt: A signal needs to travel through 3 gates before reaching a register, and the clock period is shorter than the time all 3 gates need to settle. What happens on each clock edge?
exercises.hint: the register may capture an incorrect, not-yet-settled value, since the signal hasn't finished propagating through all 3 gates before the next clock edge arrives

exercises.title: Debug a small controller
exercises.prompt: A traffic-light controller's finite-state machine is stuck permanently in the 'red' state and never transitions to 'green,' even though the timer input is confirmed to be firing correctly. What's a plausible cause?
exercises.hint: the transition logic/wiring from the 'red' state to the 'green' state on a timer-expired input may be missing, broken, or pointing back to 'red' instead of forward to 'green'

projects.title: Digital combination lock
projects.desc: Design a system that tracks an input sequence, stores state across attempts, supports reset, and produces a clear unlock output only when the correct sequence is entered.

projects.title: Four-bit arithmetic unit
projects.desc: Build a 4-bit unit supporting addition, comparison, and operation selection, with correct overflow and status-output handling.

projects.title: Traffic-light controller
projects.desc: Design a clocked finite-state machine cycling through red/yellow/green with a timed sequence, reset behavior, and a safe default state.

projects.title: Register-based mini datapath
projects.desc: Design a small datapath with multiple registers, a shared bus or explicit routing, an ALU operation, and a traceable control sequence.

projects.title: Tiny educational CPU
projects.desc: Design a small instruction set with a program counter, instruction register, general registers, and an ALU -- demonstrating fetch/decode/execute on a sample program.

projects.title: Virtual peripheral interface
projects.desc: Simulate reading a virtual sensor and controlling an output through GPIO, UART, SPI, or I²C concepts.

interviewPreparation.q: Explain, at a hardware level, what happens during one fetch-decode-execute cycle.
interviewPreparation.a: The program counter points to the next instruction's location, which is FETCHED from memory. That instruction is DECODED to determine the operation and which registers are involved. The operation is EXECUTED, typically using the ALU and datapath, and the result is stored in the destination register. The program counter then advances (or jumps), and the cycle repeats.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is a floating input a real hardware bug, and how is it fixed?
interviewPreparation.a: An input connected to nothing definite has no stable voltage and can read as noise, flickering unpredictably between 0 and 1. A pull-up or pull-down resistor gives it a defined default state so it reads reliably until something actively drives it otherwise.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the practical difference between a multiplexer and a decoder?
interviewPreparation.a: A multiplexer selects ONE of several data inputs to route to a single output, based on a select signal. A decoder takes a compact binary code and activates exactly one corresponding output line among many -- multiplexers select data, decoders activate output lines.

interviewPreparation.q: Why can't clock speed simply be increased indefinitely?
interviewPreparation.a: Every circuit has a critical path -- the slowest route a signal must travel and settle before the next clock edge. If the clock runs faster than this critical path allows, signals arrive before they've properly settled, corrupting results. Real processors are limited by exactly this constraint.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you distinguish this course's simulations from real analog circuit behavior?
interviewPreparation.a: These are deterministic, simplified digital models representing idealized on/off logic behavior -- they do not model real analog electrical characteristics like exact voltage curves, capacitance effects, or genuine semiconductor physics. That's an intentional and honest simplification for teaching digital logic concepts.

capstone.title: Build and Explain a Tiny Computer
capstone.description: Design a small, complete computer: a register set, ALU operations, a control sequence, a small instruction set, and a simple memory model -- then explain the fetch/decode/execute cycle for at least one working sample program, including test cases and known limitations.
deliverables: A simple architecture diagram showing registers, ALU, control unit, and memory connections
A defined register set and at least 4 supported instructions (e.g. LOAD, ADD, SUB, HALT)
A written fetch/decode/execute explanation, traced through at least one sample program
At least 2 test cases showing expected register values after the program runs
Debugging notes describing at least one mistake found and fixed while designing this
A README-style write-up stating clearly what the design represents (a simplified educational model) versus what it does not claim to be (a real, physically fabricated processor)
capstone.portfolioTips: Being explicit about what your design simplifies and what it doesn't claim to model is exactly the kind of honest technical communication real engineering interviews and portfolio reviews respect.

industryUsage.usage: Real CPU design starts with exactly these building blocks -- registers, ALUs, datapaths, control units -- scaled up enormously and optimized far beyond what a single course can cover, but built on the same fundamental ideas.

Real embedded hardware boards expose GPIO, UART, SPI, and I²C directly -- the exact interfaces covered in this course's Hardware Interfaces lesson, which is why this course exists as a bridge into the planned Embedded Systems course.

FPGAs let engineers configure real hardware to implement exactly the digital blocks covered in this course (adders, registers, state machines) using an HDL -- a genuinely advanced future topic this course intentionally sets realistic expectations about, rather than attempting to teach.

careerApplications: Used by computer, embedded, FPGA, and hardware-adjacent software engineers when reasoning about logic, timing, state machines, registers, buses, and hardware/software interfaces.
